summary: This RFC specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, a successor to the original 1822 protocol between hosts and the ARPANET packet switches. It lets hosts address each other with logical identifiers as well as the physical interface identifiers used by 1822.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of finding a friend only by the number on their front door, you can also call them by name, and the system works out which door that is.

questions: what is the difference between 1822 and 1822l
what is a name declaration message
what is a logical host name on the arpanet
subtitle: How ARPANET hosts could address each other by logical name instead of by the physical port they were plugged into.

tldr.problem: The original 1822 host access protocol identified a host only by its physical location (host number and IMP number), so a host could not move, share a port, use several ports or share a service name without changing its address.
tldr.mechanism: 1822L adds 16-bit logical names. Hosts declare the names they use with a Name Declaration Message, and the IMP translates a destination name to a physical port using a per-name selection policy. New 1822L leaders carry the names.
tldr.outcome: 1822 and 1822L hosts can talk to each other because the IMPs translate between the two leader styles. RFC 878 obsoletes RFC 851 and adds an appendix mapping 1822L names to IP addresses.

today: RFC 878 obsoletes RFC 851, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself describes a protocol for ARPANET hosts and IMPs.

sections.title: Why Logical Addressing
sections.content:
RFC 878 specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol (the L is for Logical), the successor to the 1822 protocol that hosts used to talk to their IMP, the packet switch they attach to. With 1822L, hosts can address each other with names that are independent of where the host is plugged into the network.

The RFC cites four advantages: referring to a host by a name independent of its location, letting different hosts share one host port on a time-division basis, letting one host use several ports (multi-homing), and letting several hosts that provide the same service share one name.

Hosts choose between 1822 and 1822L. A host declares which one it uses by the type of NOP message it sends when it comes up, and it can switch later with another NOP. The IMPs keep supporting 1822 and translate automatically, so hosts of either kind can communicate. One more difference: 1822 leaders are symmetric, so a looped-back cable looks like a legitimate message, while 1822L leaders are not, so a host can detect a looped connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Names stay the same even if a friend moves house, and one name can even belong to several friends who do the same job.

sections.title: Addresses and Names
sections.content:
Three forms of host specification exist. A 1822 address is 24 bits: an 8-bit host number and a 16-bit IMP number, used in 1822 leaders only. An 1822L name is a 16-bit unsigned number that identifies one or more hosts, except that bits 1 and 2 may not both be zero, which allows over 49,000 hosts to be specified.

An 1822L address is the subset of the name space where bits 1 and 2 are both zero. It holds a 6-bit host number and an 8-bit IMP number, so it can address hosts 0 to 63 at IMPs 1 to 255 (IMP 0 does not exist). At the time of writing the IMP had seven fake hosts, so host numbers 57 to 63 address those and 0 to 56 address real external hosts. Addresses are for reaching one specific physical port.
sections.plainLanguage: A name is like a nickname. An address is like the exact street number, for when you must reach one particular door.

sections.title: How Names Become Physical Ports
sections.content:
Names are assigned by a central network administrator, who ties each name to one or more specific host ports. Changes go out to the IMPs through the Network Operations Center. A name tied to a port this way is authorized. Only hosts on C/30 IMPs can have 1822L names; hosts on other IMPs can still use 1822L addresses to reach others.

An authorized name must also be effective before it can be used. A 1822L host sends a Name Declaration Message (NDM) listing the names it wants, and the IMP replies with an NDM Reply showing which are now effective. A host that comes up using plain 1822 gets the first name the IMP finds for it made effective when its first NOP arrives. When a host goes down, its names become non-effective.

If several hosts share a name and more than one is up, a message goes to just one of them, and the sender is not told which. Each name uses one of three pre-set selection policies: take the first reachable address in the table (the most common), take the closest physical address by least delay, or use load leveling, which starts the search after where the previous one ended.

Hosts that want to choose a port themselves can send a type 11 Name Server Request to get the full address list for a name, or a type 12 Port List Request to learn which names map to their port.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office keeps a list of who lives where. You tell it your nicknames when you arrive, and it only delivers to nicknames you are allowed to use.

sections.title: Down Hosts, Connections and Uncontrolled Packets
sections.content:
When a destination host goes down, what the source sees depends on how it addressed the host. With an 1822 address or 1822L address, or a name that maps to a single port, it gets a type 7 (Destination Host Dead) message. If the name maps to several ports, the IMP tries another effective port and, failing that, returns a type 15, subtype 5 (no effective translations) message. Messages already in flight to a named host that fails produce type 9, subtype 6 (message lost due to logically addressed host going down).

Connections for regular messages are identified by source port, source name and destination name. The destination name is translated only when a connection is opened, and at most eight messages may be outstanding on a connection. Connections time out after three minutes of inactivity. Two names for the same port can therefore yield more than one connection between the same pair of ports.

Uncontrolled packets carry names with them because they skip the normal ordering and error control. Between 1822 hosts they may hold up to 991 bits of data. With 1822L they are limited to 959 bits, and an over-long packet now produces an error indication instead of being silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: If the friend you named has gone out, the post office tells you, and if another person shares that name it tries them next.

sections.title: The 1822L Leaders
sections.content:
Each message between a host and its IMP starts with a 96-bit leader. The second, fifth and sixth words match 1822. The first word keeps the 1822 New Format Flag, which also marks the two kinds of 1822L leader, and moves the Handling Type to the second byte. The third and fourth words hold the source and destination 1822L names.

The host-to-IMP leader carries the flag value 13 in bits 5 to 8. The IMP-to-host leader carries 14. Both have a Handling Type, a Trace bit, leader flags, an 8-bit Message Type, 16-bit Source and Destination Host fields, a 12-bit Message ID with a 4-bit Sub-type, and a final word that is unused going to the IMP and a Message Length coming back.

The host source field is not filled in by the IMP, because a host may have several names and may choose which to use. Each source name is checked for authorization, effectiveness and for belonging to that host. Failures produce a type 15 error: for example subtype 0 for an unauthorized or non-effective source name, subtype 2 for an unauthorized destination name and subtype 7 when logical addressing is not in use in this network.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message wears a label with the sender's name, the receiver's name, and what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Changes and the IP Mapping Appendix
sections.content:
This RFC updates and obsoletes RFC 851. The changes are: Section 2.2.4 was rewritten for clarity, Section 2.5 was expanded on the effect of names on host-to-host virtual circuits, the type 1 IMP-to-host message gained two subtypes, the type 9 message gained one, the type 15 subtype 4 message is no longer defined, and an appendix was added.

The appendix describes how 1822L names and addresses map to internet addresses, extending the ARPANET-style mapping of RFC 796. For a class A network the upper and lower bytes of a name fill the two outer bytes of the IP host part, and a name then looks like a high-numbered (64 to 255) 1822 host. Class B networks work the same way. The appendix also notes that logical names make IMP-based class C networks possible, with internet-reachable hosts given names in the range 40000 to 40377 (octal).
sections.plainLanguage: The last part shows how the new names fit into the internet's address system so people on other networks could use them too.

fields.name: Handling Type
fields.desc: Bit 9 is the priority bit; the rest are unused.

fields.name: Trace
fields.desc: If one, the message is traced through the network.

fields.name: Leader Flags
fields.desc: Bit 22 is for the destination host; bits 23 and 24 are reserved.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: For example 0 regular, 3 NDM, 4 NOP, 11 Name Server Request, 12 Port List Request.

fields.name: Source Host
fields.desc: One of the source host's 1822L names, or its 1822L address.

fields.name: Destination Host
fields.desc: The 1822L name or address of the destination host.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Host-specified identification; bits 65 to 72 are also the Link Field.

viz.caption: TYPE 15 NAME OR ADDRESS ERROR SUBTYPES (RFC 878, SECTION 3.2)

items.label: Source name
items.desc: The Source Host 1822L name is not authorized or not effective.

items.label: Source address
items.desc: The Source Host 1822L address does not match the host port used.

items.label: Destination not authorized
items.desc: The Destination Host 1822L name is not authorized.

items.label: Not effective
items.desc: The single-homed destination host is authorized and up but not effective.

items.label: No translations
items.desc: The multi-homed destination name has no available effective translations.

items.label: Uncontrolled packet
items.desc: A logically addressed uncontrolled packet went to a dead or non-effective port.

items.label: Not in use
items.desc: Logical addressing is not in use in this network.
